name: George Francis Adams Sr.
personality: Did not bring his work home
Prioritized his wife Beryl above all else
The most important thing in his life was my Mom
notable_stories: A professional military law enforcement officer (Provost Marshall) who did not bring his work home and prioritized his wife, Beryl, above all else
Drafted for WWII: MP, self-defense instructor, Commander of POW camp holding Japanese combatants in Hawaii
Recalled for Korean War: Commander of MP detachment in Okinawa

Postings: Presidio SF (1954), Ft. Gordon GA, Frankfurt/Heidelberg (1958–62), Presidio SF (1962–), South Korea (13 months unaccompanied), retired as Provost Marshall of Ft. Lewis / Eastern Washington (1971)
1930 census listed as George F. Wells, step-son — Arthur Wells was his step-father
Arthur died when John was in 11th grade (~1963-64); Nini then moved in with John's family in San Francisco until her own death in 1967
Prior career included Union Oil / Standard Oil truck driver and St. Martin's College Olympia
Recorded correctly as step-child with surname Adams on the 1930 census (not Wells)
Cause of death confirmed: cancer, 'probably self-inflicted' — he was a moderate smoker and daily drinker (John's memoir).
He was a 'prototypical, Greatest Generation Soldier.'
Drafted first for WWII, then recalled for the Korean Conflict. After that he decided to make the Army his career.
WWII: served in Hawaii as a Military Police Officer, self-defense instructor, and Commander of a POW camp holding Japanese combatants.
Korean Conflict: Commander of the Military Police detachment in Okinawa.
First Presidio SF assignment (1954): attended San Francisco State University and finished his college degree; in charge of the stockade.
Germany (1958-62): in charge of the Military Police who rode the German trains.
Back at Presidio SF (1962): administrative job as coordinator of industrial defense on the west coast.
South Korea: assigned Provost Marshall of South Korea, went unaccompanied for 13 months.
Final assignment: Provost Marshall of Ft. Lewis and Eastern Washington, retired 1971.
Started taking family movies in Okinawa, sporadically continued through John's high school years.
At one point he told John: 'Don't expect praise. If they aren't dumping on you, you are doing just fine.'

The 1930 census taker wrongly recorded him as George F. Wells, though his relationship to the head of household was correctly given as stepson. His siblings Presley and Edith were correctly listed as stepchildren surnamed Adams.
A family photo of George and Serena shows their son (George Sr.) at about 3 years old, taken shortly before his father's death in 1920.
At the Presidio he was promoted and ran the stockade, so prisoners mowed the lawn at the family's quarters; the family got its first television and he never missed the Friday Night Fights.
When a typhoon was coming in on Okinawa, he took young John and George out into the yard and ran holding their hands while they flapped in the wind behind him.
When John was accused of breaking windows with a slingshot in Germany, his father made him prove it wasn't him ('Just the facts, mister'), which taught John to stay out of trouble.
On visits to the Simons farm in Pasco he fished the Columbia River, catching big steelhead.

On a rare fishing trip together, John tried to net a big salmon his father had fought for fifteen minutes, flipped it into the air, and it broke the line and swam off. Dad barely spoke on the way home, never told the story, and never asked John to go fishing again. Everyone else found it hilarious.
He once took both sons, John and George, for 18 holes at the Ft. Lewis Golf Course; they struggled so badly that he never asked them again.
George Sr. was a golfer who played early perimeter-weighted Lynx clubs. He was set on making John a golfer and took him, and sometimes his brother George Jr., out to the course.
George and Beryl went to the 1968 Army-Navy game weekend in Philadelphia with John and Barbara. George, an Army man, was pleased when Army won 21-14.
George Sr. was Papa to his grandsons Brian and Brendan, who spent Christmases at Nana and Papa's with cousins George, Geoffrey, Chris and Camille; he took the boys out in his boat on Puget Sound.

On the day Mount St. Helens erupted, Papa, Nana, Aunt Rosemary and Uncle Ralph drove down for Brian's First Communion; hearing the Toutle River had flooded I-5, they left at once for Olympia, and Papa talked the authorities into letting them through.
Papa made cider from the apple trees in his and Nana's front yard.
milestones: Married Beryl Simons Adams (m. 2 Jul 1942, Franklin County, WA)
Worked for Union Oil before being recalled for the Korean Conflict
Served as an MP officer in Okinawa, Germany, and the U.S.
Married Beryl Eva Simons (2 July 1942, Franklin County, WA)
Retired from U.S. Army 1971 as Provost Marshall of Ft. Lewis / Eastern Washington
Military police officer at the Presidio, San Francisco, where the family lived while John and George Jr. grew up
Census 1940: San Francisco, California, aged 24, single, stepson of Arthur T. Wells; living in Burlingame, San Mateo County, in 1935
Military: Recalled in 1952 as an Army Reservist, he commanded a company of the Military Police unit on Okinawa for almost two years; the family joined him and lived in military housing in Naha.
Military: On his way to Germany in 1958 he attended a month-long Military Police school at Fort Gordon, Georgia.
Military: In Germany he was Commanding Officer of the Military Police train riders throughout Europe, so the family had its own bodyguards whenever they rode the trains. (1958-1962)
Military: He was stationed in South Korea for all of John's senior year of high school (1964-65).
After WWII he briefly left the Army and worked for Union Oil (called Standard Oil in another chapter), and the family lived in Richmond and then Sacramento, California. (late 1940s to 1952)
In the mid-1970s, after his Army retirement, he and Beryl lived in Olympia, Washington, where Ray and Dradie Simons visited them. (mid-1970s)

In retirement he and Beryl lived near the southernmost point of Puget Sound; he took up golf again, played at the Ft. Lewis golf course, and bought a cabin cruiser that he and Beryl took out on day trips to fish for salmon. (after 1971)
Born at Mercy Hospital, Roseburg, Oregon, 10 Mar 1916
career: Before his marriage he drove truck for Union Oil, then enrolled at St. Martin's College in Olympia and worked at a filling station. (about 1941-1942)

notes: Referenced in Brendan McKeldin Adams: Paternal grandparents are Beryl Adams and George Francis Adams II
Also referred to as George Francis Adams Sr. Siblings listed: Presley Marcason, Edith V.
Marriage to Beryl Eva Simons: 2 July 1942, Franklin County, WA — confirmed.
Rosemary Wells was his step-sister (Arthur Wells' biological daughter, ~1916), raised essentially as his sister. Prior source had birth listed as 10 Mar 1916 — confirmed here.
Cause of death: cancer, moderate smoker and daily drinker (John's memoir). Confirms 1980 death.
Pictured as 'George Jr.' in a c. 1919 family photograph with George F., Serena, Edith and Presley [Bill Allen, Descendants of Jose Pierre Adams, 2011, line 6079]
As George Adams, he appears in a census in the household of his stepfather Arthur T. Wells, after his father's death. [Family research emails, email 17]

He was always known as 'Sr.' rather than III; his son George writes that technically he was George II, because of a generation gap between the first two George Francis Adamses. [Family research emails, email 31]

The 1920 census of his parents' household in Douglas County, Oregon, lists a son "Edward G. Adams", aged 3 years 9 months (born about 1916-17, Oregon), and no other young son; George, born 10 Mar 1916, would have been 3 years 10 months. [1920 U.S. census, Douglas County, Oregon, household 51, sheet 9 (FamilySearch index, accessed 2 Apr 2013)]

CORRECTION 2026-09-24: His Oregon birth certificate (no. 25) records George Francis Adams, born 10 Mar 1916 at Mercy Hospital, Roseburg, the third child of George Francis Adams, druggist, and Serena Trumbo, of Sutherlin. The given name was added by a supplemental report on 25 Mar 1916, so he was named George Francis two weeks after birth, not renamed after his father's death. No certificate exists for an Edward G. Adams. The "Edward G. Adams", aged 3, in the 1920 census is the only young son in the household, and in 1930 he appears as George F., 14, stepson of Arthur T. Wells, with Presley and Edith, so "Edward G." looks like the enumerator's error or a family name.
His father died on 7 Feb 1920 (Oregon death index), when George was nearly 4, not in 1918 when he was 2.
He died on 11 Oct 1980 at Tacoma, Washington (Find a Grave, memorial 239144218).
